Resilient

rih-ZIL-yent — the root means 'to leap'; a resilient person leaps right back after being knocked down. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Resilient is able to recover quickly from difficulty; tough enough to spring back instead of breaking in hard times.

Despite losing everything in the flood, the resilient community rebuilt its homes within a year.

Worked Example

A young athlete tears a ligament just months before the biggest competition of her career, yet through months of grueling physical therapy she not only returns to the sport but eventually breaks her own personal record.

Bouncing back from a serious setback stronger than before is exactly what resilient means. Unlike 'lucky,' which implies chance, resilient describes real inner toughness and the ability to recover.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

hardy: Hardy means built to endure harsh conditions -- a hardy plant survives frost, a hardy hiker shrugs off cold. Resilient is about what happens after damage actually lands: being hurt and then springing back. A hardy thing barely feels the hardship; a resilient one recovers from it.

durable: Durable describes objects and materials that resist wear and keep working for a long time -- durable boots, a durable phone case. Resilient is about recovery: a resilient person or community takes a real blow and springs back. Durable things avoid damage; resilient ones recover from it.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

fragile: easily broken or damaged

vulnerable: easily harmed or affected

Where it sits · from enduring harm to adjusting fully — tough → resilient → adaptable

tough vs. resilient: Tough is a more general word than resilient -- something tough simply resists damage, while resilient specifically emphasizes bouncing back and recovering after hardship strikes.

adaptable vs. resilient: Adaptable can feel broader than resilient: resilient focuses on recovering from a setback, while adaptable means adjusting successfully to any new or changing situation, setback or not.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — re-

prefix — re-: back (Latin)

root — -sil-

root — -sil-: to leap (Latin (salire))

suffix — -ient

suffix — -ient: doing or being; forms an adjective (variant of -ent) (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin resilire meant 'to leap back,' from re- ('back') plus salire ('to leap'), and the suffix -ient makes it an adjective. A resilient person is literally 'leaping back' -- bouncing back from hardship rather than staying down.
